newsitem.title: USA: Freeh says no progress on Olympic leak probe.
newsitem.headline: Freeh says no progress on Olympic leak probe.

text.p: FBI Director Louis Freeh said on Thursday any agent found to have leaked security guard Richard Jewell's name to the news media as a suspect in the Atlanta Olympics bombing would probably be fired.

But Freeh told a Senate hearing there had been no progress in an investigation to find out who disclosed Jewell's name as the chief suspect in the July 27 blast that killed two people and injured more than 100 in Atlanta's Olympic park.

"I have a zero tolerance policy for the unauthorised release of information," he told the Senate Judiciary Committee. "If we find a deliberate leak without any mitigating circumstances that person will be fired."

Freeh said he had sent several messages to all FBI employees warning they would be punished for disclosing information. He said several agents were disciplined in recent years for unauthorised comments but only one had been fired.

At least 500 people in the FBI and nine other law enforcement agencies knew that Jewell was a suspect, Freeh said. Asked if there had been any progress in investigating the leak, he replied, "No sir."

Jewell, a security guard at the park, was first hailed as a hero for spotting the knapsack containing the bomb and warning many people away before the explosion. But he was identified as a suspect a few days later and was followed and watched by the news media for the next three months.
He was cleared as a suspect by the Justice Department in October and is considering a suit against the government.

A separate investigation is being conducted into the way agents questioned Jewell. After he was named in news reports, two agents asked him to come to the FBI's Atlanta office to help make a training film on how to question a witness.

During the videotaped session, one agent told Jewell he wanted the film to be realistic and asked him to sign a waiver of his rights to remain silent and to have a lawyer present. Jewell refused and asked to call a lawyer.

Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Democrat from Vermont, said he was concerned about the way Jewell was treated. "To the extent that one or more FBI agents suffered from 'loose lips' about the Atlanta bombing investigation I am sure that this director will get to the bottom of it," Leahy said.
Freeh said he did not fault the media for reporting leaked information. He said most newspapers and broadcasters cooperated when asked to withhold information about an ongoing investigation.

Asked if focusing on Jewell hampered the investigation of who put the bomb in the park, Freeh said, "I would certainly say it was a distraction to the investigation. It had an adverse impact. I don't think it was a significant impact."

The FBI last week offered a $500,000 reward for information about the bombing and asked anyone who was at the park that night to provide any pictures or videotapes that might show the bomber. Freeh said the FBI had received hundreds of leads that were being checked.
